text.p: Big retailers who offer low prices and wide selection have won out over local neighbourhood stores, leading to vast changes in the retailing landscape over the past 25 years, a leading research firm said Tuesday.

While nostalgic images of mom 'n' pop stores and luncheonettes loom large in the American dream, larger stores have all but buried them, according to the 1996 Annual National Retail Census by Audits & Surveys Worldwide of New York, which surveyed 35,000 retail outlets in 800 geographic areas.

The survey found that dramatic shifts in consumer behaviour, combined with mergers and acquisitions, have transformed American retailing over the last 25 years, not merely in big, regional malls but also in neighbourhoods.

Gas stations are on the wane, while used-car dealerships have mushroomed, according to the report obtained by Reuters. There are fewer luncheonettes but many more fast-food restaurants. Discount stores are outstripping department stores, and dime stores like Woolworth's and catalogue showrooms are swiftly on the way out.
As household appliance stores have declined, the number of radio-television-stereo stores has risen sharply. There are many more book, jewelry, sporting goods and liquor stores.
"U.S consumers may be nostalgic about small, independent retailers but not enough to patronise them," said Solomon Dutka, chief executive of Audits & Surveys.
"In one retailing sector after another, consumers willingly sacrificed location, personal service and expertise for the amenities that matter most to them: low prices and big selections," he said.

The prescription for success, Dutka added, "is that small retailers must get big enough to achieve competitive economies of scale or agile enough to find a niche and hold on to it if they are to survive."

In food retailing, casualties are rampant among luncheonettes (down 25 percent to 55,860), taverns and bars (down 40 percent to 66,230) and food stores in general (off 27 percent to 140,000). The franchise system and marketing prowess of fast-food restaurants, which have grown 158 percent over the past 25 years to 129,280 outlets, have hurt the sit-down luncheonettes.

Audits & Surveys attributes the decline in taverns and bars to a slump in the "consumption of beer and distilled spirits as a result of health concerns and lifestyle changes." But the number of restaurants offering table service is about the same as in 1970, 88,550.

Pressured by supermarket chains and small convenience stores, the number of independent neighbourhood groceries and supermarkets has shrunk 16 percent to 68,950. Independent drugstores have also been hurt, mainly because of "the growth of large chain stores, which has accelerated, adding 12 percent more outlets in the last five years alone," the report said.
But convenience store numbers have soared a dramatic 50.3 percent since 1980 to 53,580, boosted by rapid growth, high traffic, neighbourhood locations and long store opening hours,

Although discount stores have carved a broad, deep swath, up 109 percent in number since 1970 to 8,700 stores, their growth halted in 1996 as "past success left little room for additional market penetration," the report said.
Department stores, hurt by discounters and speciality stores and pared by acquisitions and consolidations, are down 16.1 percent from 1970 to 5,190 and off 6 percent in the last five years alone.

The rise of the huge do-it-yourself store chains took a major toll on hardware and building materials stores. Since 1970, hardware has dropped 25 percent to 21,790 stores. Paint, glass and wallpaper stores are down 9 percent to 10,760 and lumber and building supply stores are down 10 percent to 23,200. Meanwhile, home centres or big-store discounters which sell to contractors as well as consumers grew 22 percent since 1980 to 10,790 units.

Megastores have invaded other sectors as well, since "it pays to specialise," Audits & Surveys said. The number of radio-television-stereo stores surged 128 percent to 26,950 outlets, while recorded music and musical instruments stores rose 46 percent to 13,260.

Expansion and market entry by national and international speciality operators provided new muscle to apparel store chains, but independent stores were hurt. The number of such stores has fallen in the last two years to 166,920 stores, but the total is still 45 percent more than in 1970.
